analysis.one_liner: Requires the Justice Department to collect and publish national data on police brutality complaints.
analysis.headline: A bill to make the Justice Department publish annual national data on police brutality complaints was referred to a House subcommittee in 1992 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Attorney General to gather nationwide data on the number, nature, and outcome of police brutality complaints — including complaints of excessive force based on race, religion, or ethnicity — and on how federal, state, and local governments investigate those complaints [S2] [S3]. The Justice Department would have to publish a yearly public summary, recommend ways to stop complaints from being dismissed after inadequate investigation, and issue model procedures that departments could adopt [S2] [S3]. It was a transparency bill: it created no new penalties and no new police powers, just public reporting and recommendations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who file or consider filing excessive-force complaints, civil rights groups, and researchers, because complaint data would be collected and published nationally for the first time, making it possible to see which departments dismiss complaints after inadequate investigation and what better procedures look like [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The Attorney General would have to acquire national data on the number, nature, and disposition of police brutality complaints and on the procedures governments use to investigate and resolve them [S2] [S3].
An annual public summary of that data would be published, and the recommendations and model procedures would have to be made available to the public at reasonable cost [S3].

The recommendations were required to include methods that discourage the suppression and summary dismissal of complaints after inadequate investigation — the central mechanism by which misconduct complaints typically go nowhere [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, which would bear the burden of reporting complaint data and would face public scrutiny of how they handle brutality complaints. Taxpayers would fund the Justice Department's data collection. The bill contains no new penalties, so the cost is mostly administrative.

drawbacks.text: The bill is advisory only: it creates no penalties for departments that fail to report or that suppress complaints, and its recommendations are nonbinding, so it relies entirely on publicity and voluntary adoption to change behavior [S2] [S3].

Data collection under 28 U.S.C. 534 depends on cooperation from state and local agencies; the bill does not clearly compel local departments to supply complaint data, so national coverage could be incomplete [S3].
It adds federal paperwork requirements for state and local governments, a cost its critics would cite, without any direct enforcement power attached [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, well-designed transparency measure: the cost to taxpayers is small, and annual public data on brutality complaints would give citizens, journalists, and officials a way to see which departments dismiss complaints. But its design is soft — no penalties, no mandate on local departments, purely advisory recommendations — so even if enacted it would likely have shifted behavior slowly. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs, which makes its quiet death without a vote more notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, forwarded to its crime subcommittee nearly a year later, and never came back out for a committee vote or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kweisi Mfume introduced the Police Brutality Accountability Act of 1991 on April 17, 1991, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1] [S5].
Six Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on [S4].
On March 18, 1992, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, a step from which most bills never emerge, and no markup or vote ever followed [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died with it, never having received a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and other law enforcement agencies are better off: they were never required to report brutality complaint data nationally or face public comparison of how they resolve complaints. Citizens gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies, which avoided public scrutiny

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote: after a year it was sent to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, and no markup was ever scheduled [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no party breakdown exists; the only recorded support was seven House Democrats (the sponsor and six cosponsors), with no Republicans listed [S4].

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local police departments)
industries.note: The bill would have required national reporting of brutality complaints and public annual summaries, exposing departments whose complaint-handling is weak, including those that dismiss complaints after inadequate investigation [S2] [S3]. The cost to these agencies is administrative and reputational rather than financial, and their interest in avoiding public complaint data runs directly against the public's interest in accountability. The record shows no legislative movement to fight it — the bill simply never got a hearing or vote [S5].
